headline: Steam, Not Chemicals, Now Grows Organic Strawberries in California
meta_description: UC Santa Cruz researchers prove steam fumigation can replace toxic chemicals in organic strawberry farming, giving growers a safer, more reliable alternative.
summary_short: Researchers at UC Santa Cruz have shown that steam can effectively replace harmful chemical fumigants in organic strawberry farming, offering growers a safer path to rel…
body:
Researchers at the University of California Santa Cruz have discovered that injecting steam into soil before planting strawberries can replace the toxic chemical fumigants that have long been the industry standard—offering organic growers a way to sterilize their fields without compromising their certification or risking bankruptcy. In a recent trial involving four organic strawberry farmers, including longtime grower Rod Koda, the steam-treated beds produced bigger, healthier plants and significantly more strawberries. The steam kills the soil bacteria, fungi, and weeds that can devastate crops, particularly fusarium wilt, a disease that has historically forced organic farmers to either gamble with their harvests or abandon traditional growing for hydroponics.

The innovation, while appearing novel in agricultural soil, actually builds on a technology greenhouse operators have used for decades. As UCSC researcher Jenny Broome explained, the team is essentially "going back to the future"—refining an older method through modern engineering to make it more efficient and practical at scale. The timing matters enormously: strawberries account for one of California's largest and most valuable crops, with some 35,000 acres dedicated to cultivation. For organic growers tending these delicate plants so vulnerable to pests, the steam method offers something that has been missing—a reliable, chemical-free path forward that doesn't require choosing between environmental responsibility and economic survival.

This development joins other recent innovations aimed at making organic strawberry farming more viable, from military-grade textiles that triple yields by excluding insects while allowing sunlight and moisture through. As demand for organic produce grows, simple solutions grounded in proven science may prove just as valuable as high-tech alternatives.
quick_facts: UC Santa Cruz researchers tested steam fumigation with four organic strawberry farmers
Steam kills soil-borne fungi, bacteria, and weeds that damage strawberry plants
California grows strawberries on approximately 35,000 acres
Greenhouse operators have used steam as a pesticide for decades
